item.title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
item.description: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government. The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters. The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month. A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers. For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected. While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand. At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens. In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US. Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators. Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless. Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not. What the judgment does not confirm While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public. "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers. For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected. While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand. At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens. In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US. Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators. Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless. Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not. What the judgment does not confirm While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public. "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest. "We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed. "That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now." The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026. The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users. The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty , Privacy International , and two individuals. A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public. "A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data. "Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so. "Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies." Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

item.title: Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in
item.description: A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2. The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again." Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored." Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID. Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected. An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets. Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057 , the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

item.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
item.description: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme Continue reading...

item.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
item.description: null An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all? Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. Lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process." This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data. That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein. Take it away Einstein Einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature. The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. item.dc:creator: Robert Lea
item.content:encoded: null An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all? Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. Lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process." This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data. That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein. Take it away Einstein Einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature. The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. Around this would be a spherical boundary at which not even light has the velocity needed to escape this region. Referred to as the Schwarzschild radius, that boundary became known as the event horizon of a black hole. The singularity, its heart. Black holes were born in 1915, decades before their discovery and over a century before the EHT saw one. An illustration of Einstein and a supermassive black hole (Image credit: Robert Lea) General relativity also predicted what the region around the event horizon would look like. A ring of superheated glowing plasma with the shadow of the black hole falling on it. When scientists first saw the image of M87* they were astounded at how close it reflected predictions made by general relativity, thus confirming the the theory once again. This verification further solidifies that development. Verifying the EHT's image of M87* could lead to the CSIRO-developed technique being applied to some more "down-to-Earth" uses such as improving medical imaging and mapping earthquakes. "Independent validation is at the heart of the scientific process, and it is especially valuable for results as novel as those of the EHT. It is extremely gratifying to see that GenDIReCT, an elegant, entirely independent method, recovers the ring structure of M87* across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration’s published results," Laurent Loinard, Director of the EHT Collaboration, said. "Studies like this strengthen our confidence in what we have learned about black holes, and enrich the toolkit available to the whole community." The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature.

item.title: SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule returns to Earth from the ISS
item.description: null SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has come home to Earth. The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov. 20) at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China. The freighter made its way Earthward over the next 29 hours, ultimately splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at 5:03 p.m. EST (2155 GMT). The Dragon launched Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it was the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program. The capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15 , delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It brought a lot of stuff down to Earth, too. "Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an update on Tuesday (Nov. 17). "The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth ," they added. Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight. Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 20 with news of successful undocking, then again at 8:55 p.m. ET on Nov. 21 with news of splashdown.

item.title: Ubuntu Core Desktop targets 28.04 debut, with default status in its sights
item.description: Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04. Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. Yes, we know, we have heard this before: we reported on his plans last month . But this time, there's the beginning of a release schedule. Seager said that Ubuntu Core is already out there in tens of thousands of IoT devices – which seems like a modest estimate to us, and to him too, as he quickly added "maybe more." Despite some noise a few years ago, though, what's still missing is the desktop version. Seager's slides listed three bullet points: that Core Desktop will be "immutable," "composable," and "attestable." As he put it, they are "taking the whole of the Linux operating system, and cramming the whole thing into snaps." Acknowledging that this is going to be wildly controversial, he said: "This is one for the Redditors." He's right. There is a lot of resistance to snap, and in direct response, advocacy of the Red Hat-backed Flatpak instead – but we have seen almost none that is based on either system's technical merits. Much of that opposition concerns claims of one being more open than the other. We've looked at how both systems work, and our impression is that the implementation of snap is cleaner, simpler, easier to use, and more comprehensible. Snap does depend on systemd, which Flatpak does not – but only for now. Flatpak NG is in development and will also need everyone's favorite init system. Ubuntu Core's immutability is not new technology: even Core 16 is now a decade old. It has supported in-place version upgrades since Core 22. We have reported before that Canonical remains strongly committed to its packaging format, and that commitment seems stronger than ever. Seager continued: "Never has a model like snap confinement been more relevant… we're finally in a position where we can bring this to the desktop." The core idea of an immutable OS is that "much more of the system is not writable at runtime," meaning that it "can't be messed with once the system has booted." He talked about the same three use cases we discussed last month. The "browser-centric machine" is the company's analog to Google ChromeOS, and he said that it's essentially ready now, suggesting that everyone listening probably has a family member whose computer is basically just a way to use a web browser. The second was the dedicated games machine, which we interpret as a response to Valve's SteamOS. This edition, he said, would "boot straight to Steam," with "just enough of a shell to launch games." There's also an immutable "development workstation," and here, he offered the example of developers who need to work on some long-unsupported hardware or software, for whom an immutable OS means that you "can't brick your system by installing some weird old dependencies, unmaintained for 20 years." item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04. Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. Yes, we know, we have heard this before: we reported on his plans last month . But this time, there's the beginning of a release schedule. Seager said that Ubuntu Core is already out there in tens of thousands of IoT devices – which seems like a modest estimate to us, and to him too, as he quickly added "maybe more." Despite some noise a few years ago, though, what's still missing is the desktop version. Seager's slides listed three bullet points: that Core Desktop will be "immutable," "composable," and "attestable." As he put it, they are "taking the whole of the Linux operating system, and cramming the whole thing into snaps." Acknowledging that this is going to be wildly controversial, he said: "This is one for the Redditors." He's right. There is a lot of resistance to snap, and in direct response, advocacy of the Red Hat-backed Flatpak instead – but we have seen almost none that is based on either system's technical merits. Much of that opposition concerns claims of one being more open than the other. We've looked at how both systems work, and our impression is that the implementation of snap is cleaner, simpler, easier to use, and more comprehensible. Snap does depend on systemd, which Flatpak does not – but only for now. Flatpak NG is in development and will also need everyone's favorite init system. Ubuntu Core's immutability is not new technology: even Core 16 is now a decade old. It has supported in-place version upgrades since Core 22. We have reported before that Canonical remains strongly committed to its packaging format, and that commitment seems stronger than ever. Seager continued: "Never has a model like snap confinement been more relevant… we're finally in a position where we can bring this to the desktop." The core idea of an immutable OS is that "much more of the system is not writable at runtime," meaning that it "can't be messed with once the system has booted." He talked about the same three use cases we discussed last month. The "browser-centric machine" is the company's analog to Google ChromeOS, and he said that it's essentially ready now, suggesting that everyone listening probably has a family member whose computer is basically just a way to use a web browser. The second was the dedicated games machine, which we interpret as a response to Valve's SteamOS. This edition, he said, would "boot straight to Steam," with "just enough of a shell to launch games." There's also an immutable "development workstation," and here, he offered the example of developers who need to work on some long-unsupported hardware or software, for whom an immutable OS means that you "can't brick your system by installing some weird old dependencies, unmaintained for 20 years." Another important benefit is "atomic, transactional updates," which he said "brings enormous stability." The terminology comes from the database world : an atomic operation succeeds as a whole or is not applied. The aim is to avoid leaving the system stranded between incompatible package versions, with rollback providing a route back if an update causes trouble. The "composable" part means assembling the OS from separately packaged components, from desktop environments to underlying services such as PipeWire and fingerprint-reader support. Here, Seager used an example that spoke to us. He asked: "Ever installed something and watch as it spewed stuff all over your system?" Yes, we have, many, many times. You install one innocent-seeming little component, and it brings in a database, three new server components, and about half of a different desktop environment. We mentioned an example when we described how to customize Xfce a couple of months ago. That time around, in Debian, we found it was safe to install all packages starting with "xfce4-" except "xfce4-dev-tools." Most are tiny panel controls taking just hundreds of kilobytes, but the "dev-tools" package also pulls in several hundred megabytes of compilers, linkers, and other programming tools, totally unrelated to desktop layouts – and once installed, they're surprisingly tricky to remove again. This is part of the appeal of a composable immutable OS: adding a component need not mean tangling its dependencies into the base system. But easier housekeeping isn't the only attraction. Canonical kept snap packages from its cancelled phone and tablet OS because snaps enable it to maintain a single package of, for instance, Firefox, which will work on all of its different OS versions that are still getting updates. Moving such important external dependencies into isolated snap packages makes it easier and safer to upgrade from one version of the OS to another. Complex sets of dependencies are the main point of failure of OS upgrades, especially when the OS has been used for a while. This is very much not a solved problem. For instance, Debian version upgrades can be fraught – especially when the installation has decades of history behind it . Debian does at least support version-to-version upgrades. For many years and versions, RHEL did not – which is why we highlighted AlmaLinux's tooling for the task . Zorin OS added version-to-version upgrades in 16.3 just a few years ago. Linux Mint introduced its own upgrade tooling a few years earlier, although it still imposes restrictions . It's a tough issue to crack. Major enterprise vendors discourage it, and phone OSes are all immutable. Helping with this problem is one of the main reasons snap packaging exists, while Flatpak is almost entirely irrelevant to it. Seager also stated that Core Desktop would support "multiple desktops from the start." This will not be a GNOME-only project. Indeed, he specifically mentioned a KDE Plasma version, saying: "Plasma is great. People love it. We will have a KDE edition, with rolling Plasma. We will deliver upstream Plasma, as fast as we can." That sounds like a very welcome counterpoint to the LTS version of Plasma 6.6 in Kubuntu 26.04 whose announcement we covered back in August. For the "attestable" line of the slide, he claimed that Core Desktop was "evolving the way we think about 'trust' on a machine. We have TPM, secure boot, TPM-backed Full Disk Encryption… but they're all bolt-ons." Core Desktop, he added, could "tie this into a hardware root of trust," delivering "verified system integrity." Canonical revived its TPM-backed full-disk encryption system back in 2025 , and it arrived in Ubuntu 26.04. Back in January, systemd creator Lennart Poettering launched his startup Amutable, and earlier this month published a technical overview of its new immutable Linux . We suspect Canonical is watching closely, and that this is a hint in that direction. We were also amused by Seager's mention of another rather niche distro: he said that Core Desktop would deliver "all of the joy that people derive from NixOS, for those with that perverse habit – but for everybody." Daily preview installation images of Core Desktop will, apparently, be available very soon, in both GNOME and KDE flavors, and he warned that "there be dragons." (That may be a veiled nod to one of founder Mark Shuttleworth's other companies .) After the promises made in 2023 , we'll be watching that timetable closely. "I believe this is the future of Linux," Seager said, promising "a final version by 28.04, released alongside Ubuntu," adding that a "very stretchy stretch goal was by default for 30.04: download from ubuntu.com and you get Core Desktop – unless you ask for the other thing." For those alarmed by that prospect, he had reassurance: "Ubuntu as you know it today is not going anywhere. There are no plans for the existing distro to go away." item.title: Support tech fixed malware by charging client less for their services
item.description: Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call , The Register 's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city. "I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends." The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits. Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC. "I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time. "He actually said, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'." Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself! "It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product." So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers. Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact. "I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!" Have you done less tech support to deliver more value? If so, click here to send On Call an email and charge us with the responsibility of telling your story on a future Friday. ®

item.title: From Dancehall to Rumba, Rema Stretches His Sound on New EP “E-Mortal Boy (EMB)” | Listen
item.description: Rema releases his seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy (EMB), featuring Wizkid, Theodora, BNYX, and Kah-Lo. Photo Credit: Rema/Instagram For weeks, Rema has been teasing us with a new project—first came “ TEA ” and then “ Oh No “, and if you have had those on repeat on your playlist, you now have the entire package with his seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy ( EMB ). Ever since his self-titled debut EP in 2019, the Benin-born star has never been interested in staying boxed into one sound. Following his 2023 EP Ravage and his 2024 Grammy-nominated album HEIS , he uses this new seven-song collection to pull rhythms from across the Black diaspora into one bold, genre-hopping ride. If you already had “TEA” on loop when its dancehall bounce, glossy pop, and techno twists took over the Nigerian timeline, or kept “Oh No” close for that percussion-heavy Rvssian groove about a lover’s mixed signals, they both sit right inside the full lineup alongside five more records . The biggest headline moment opens the project: “ Feel Alright ” pairs Rema with Wizkid for their very first official joint release, a smooth ballad about satisfying a lover’s appetite. From there, he switches gears across “ Velvet “, where rumba drums meet slick guitar riffs as he vows to take on the world for someone special, and “ TANZANIA “, a BNYX-assisted track with Bollywood score-inspired flair. The rest of the EP keeps that same adventurous streak alive. On “ SUGA “, Rema teams up with French Congolese singer Theodora for a rougher, grunge-leaning sound, before closing out on “ Bang Bang ” with longtime collaborator London and Nigerian dance music favourite Kah-Lo . Nearly a decade into his run, Rema still sounds completely locked in on what comes next, leaving you with seven quick tracks to drop straight into your weekend rotation. Listen below ﻿ The post From Dancehall to Rumba, Rema Stretches His Sound on New EP “E-Mortal Boy (EMB)” | Listen appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Big Tech's compliance with EU market rules is performative, consumer group says
item.description: Big Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice. BEUC said : "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products." The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023 , imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition. The devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on. BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026. In the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the company used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from users for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine. "Microsoft also regularly prompts users who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC said. Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store users to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications. The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge users into handing over their data. item.dc:creator: Richard Speed
item.content:encoded: Big Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice. BEUC said : "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products." The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023 , imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition. The devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on. BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026. In the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the company used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from users for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine. "Microsoft also regularly prompts users who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC said. Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store users to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications. The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge users into handing over their data. Apple announced new terms for developers earlier this year in response to its App Store dispute with the European Commission, but BEUC said it was "concerned that the new terms do not resolve fundamental non-compliance issues." Google did not respond to requests for comment from The Register . A Microsoft spokesperson told us: "We are continuing to engage with the Commission and industry at large to ensure Microsoft's designated platforms comply fully with the DMA." An Amazon spokesperson told The Register “Our consent experience is clear and gives customers informed choice about how their personal information is used across Amazon services. We see that in practice. “A seller that uses Amazon Stores in the EU can offer the same products on any third-party online marketplace or its own direct to customer website at any price, without affecting their eligibility to be highlighted as the Featured Offer. This is set out clearly in our DMA Compliance Report.” BEUC director general Agustín Reyna said: "The era of cosmetic compliance must end. It is high time the Commission holds gatekeepers to account and imposes dissuasive penalties in all cases where they bypass the DMA's rules." The report has been shared with the Commission. Whether BEUC's allegations lead to further findings of non-compliance or penalties is now a matter for the regulator. ®

item.title: Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone
item.description: null PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth , something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary. Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2 , flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate Voyager 1 's distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space. "I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker said during Thursday's event. An unexpected, but manageable, anomaly While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning. Unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the issue, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon. NASA and Voyager team members celebrate Voyager 1's light-day milestone at NASA JPL on Nov. 19, 2026. From left to right: Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate; Jonathan Lunine, chief scientist, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager; Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager; Jamie Rankin, Voyager deputy project scientist. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd) "We listen to each spacecraft every day," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd told Space.com at the event. Regarding Voyager 1, "we have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," Dodd said. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We currently don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently." "But if you recall," Dodd added, "one light-day is very far from us. [It takes] 24 hours to get the signal to the spacecraft, 24 hours for the signal to come down, so it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft … So we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low." item.dc:creator: Chelsea Gohd
item.content:encoded: null PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth , something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary. Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2 , flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate Voyager 1 's distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space. "I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker said during Thursday's event. An unexpected, but manageable, anomaly While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning. Unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the issue, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon. NASA and Voyager team members celebrate Voyager 1's light-day milestone at NASA JPL on Nov. 19, 2026. From left to right: Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate; Jonathan Lunine, chief scientist, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager; Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager; Jamie Rankin, Voyager deputy project scientist. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd) "We listen to each spacecraft every day," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd told Space.com at the event. Regarding Voyager 1, "we have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," Dodd said. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We currently don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently." "But if you recall," Dodd added, "one light-day is very far from us. [It takes] 24 hours to get the signal to the spacecraft, 24 hours for the signal to come down, so it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft … So we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low." According to Dodd, this anomaly isn't a major cause for long-term concern. Rather, it's likely just part of the natural aging process for spacecraft. "These spacecraft are old," she said. "All of us old people have our aches and pains, and you know, sometimes it takes longer to stretch out your muscles and remember things, and so we are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager just due to the distance and the age." "But we feel Voyager 1, although it's not sending us the telemetry data, it's pointed at the Earth . It's sending us a strong carrier signal, and I'm confident that it won't be too long, and it will send us data back." And, for anyone curious how Voyager 1's slower twin Voyager 2 is faring, Dodd shared that it is doing very well on its own journey through interstellar space . "Voyager 2 is very healthy. It's continuing its mission. It has three scientific instruments on it," she told Space.com. "Each spacecraft is basically setting a record every day for longevity or distance," Dodd added about the twin probes. A Voyager 1 photo of Saturn, which the probe flew by in November 1980. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) A heartfelt celebration Despite the communications anomaly — and even though most of the team had been up all night to confirm the one-light-day signal from Voyager 1 — the room was alive with excitement. The Voyagers have been flying for nearly 50 years on a mission expected to last just five years, so the team was beyond ready to celebrate. Amidst the more technical updates about the mission and its current status out in interstellar space, the event included footage of Voyager light-day celebrations from around the world. From children cheering on Voyager to iconic landmarks lighting up gold in honor of the mission's Golden Record, the Voyager love echoed around the world in photos and videos. The footage of this international celebration was enough to move Nicky Fox, NASA's associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate, nearly to tears. "I actually thought I was going to start sobbing," Fox joked to Space.com after the media briefing. "I think just hearing children's voices and people saying 'We love you, Voyager,' 'Go Voyager' — it just was amazing." And Fox and the mission team members weren't the only ones sharing their love for Voyager. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins beamed down her own video message to the Voyager 1 spacecraft from the International Space Station , sharing in the celebration. "Dear Voyager 1," Watkins said. "As an orbiting outpost just 250 miles [400 kilometers] above Earth, we often feel distant yet deeply connected to our home planet. The International Space Station has had crew continuously living off of the Earth for 26 years, seen hundreds of visitors from around the world, and enabled thousands of experiments to advance space exploration. "While you have been traveling into the unknown for nearly half a century, helping pave our path, together, our two journeys tell a single story of exploration," she continued. "One remains close to home, and the other reaches ever outward. Voyager 1, you have been a beacon of light, a symbol of exploration, a seeker of truth, a carrier of hope, a brave explorer, traveling further than any human hand has ever reached. You represent the very best of what humanity has to offer. "As you reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, the entire crew of Expedition 75 and people across the planet send you our admiration and our wishes for a safe and continued journey as you begin your post-one-light-day era. There are so many amazing milestones and discoveries to come. You have a universe ahead of you, and you carry with you our collective hopes and dreams. When we look up from Earth, we will always think of you as you continue forward into the great unknown. May you continue shining bright for all of us. Go Voyager 1!" Watkins said, ending her message with a weightless backflip from aboard the station. In concluding the media briefing, the mission team invited those in the room who, over the past 50 years (or more, with one person sharing their excitement having worked on Voyager before it was even called Voyager) have worked on the mission in one way or another, to stand up to a round of applause. With mission team members today ranging from those in their 20s to their 90s, the people behind this enduring mission span many generations. A golden moment Interestingly, Fox actually began her light-day celebrations earlier in the week. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
item.description: null On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa. An artist's illustration of Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft landing on asteroid Itokawa. (Image credit: JAXA) Why it mattered The primary goal of Japan's Hayabusa mission to asteroid Itokawa was never to be the first spacecraft to liftoff from a space rock. The mission was always aimed at collecting samples from an asteroid and returning them to Earth. It was a hard road to Itokawa for Hayabusa. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched the probe on May 9, 2003, with plans for an arrival at the asteroid in the early summer of 2005. That asteroid arrival was delayed until September 2005 after a solar storm degraded Hayabusa's solar arrays, limiting the available power for its ion engines. The asteroid Itokawa as seen by Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft. (Image credit: JAXA) Still, Hayabusa managed to limp along its path to reach the asteroid Itokawa on Sept. 12, 2005. Hayabusa dropped a small lander onto Itokawa, but that probe was apparently lost. Hayabusa then dropped a landing target on the asteroid, and ultimately managed to touchdown about 99 feet from the marker, JAXA has said. During its first landing on Nov. 19, Hayabusa descended to a point just 56 feet above Itokawa before going silent for 3 hours, according to an Associated Press report . Once contact was restored, JAXA officials confirmed the probe had landed, and it eventually lifted off for a second attempt. That was the first-ever liftoff from an asteroid by a spacecraft. "The spacecraft actually bounced off the surface a few times and spent about 39 minutes resting on the asteroid, but apparently the samplers never fired," Andrew Cheng, a Hayabusa science team member at Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, told Space.com at the time . There was hope that some material managed to make it inside the collector anyway. "After all the thrashing about ... there is no way to confirm that," Cheng had said. The second landing on Itokawa occured a few days later on Nov. 26, 2005. item.title: The view from the tower: Watch Starship come in for chopsticks catch in epic slo-mo video
item.description: null A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage. The company notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms. You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar. But on Tuesday (Nov. 17), SpaceX released up-close views — a series of four slo-mo videos captured by cameras near the top of the 480-foot-tall (146 meters) tower. The Ship upper stage of SpaceX's Starship megarocket comes back to its launch tower for a "chopsticks" catch on Nov. 14, 2026, during the vehicle's 15th test flight. (Image credit: SpaceX) "The Starbase tower chopsticks catching their first Starship. This unique architecture was designed for full and rapid reusability, enabling repeat launches and landings from the same pad," SpaceX wrote in a Tuesday X post that shared the videos, a compilation of which you can see embedded above. Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. Its current "V3" version stands about 408 feet (124 m) tall, and future iterations will be even larger . As SpaceX noted in Tuesday's post, the megarocket is also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first for an orbital launch system. The company plans to catch both Starship stages — Ship and the Super Heavy booster — at the launch tower, a recovery strategy designed to enable efficient inspection, refurbishment and reflight. Another view of the chopsticks catch on Nov. 14. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX planned to carry out such a double catch on this most recent test flight , Starship's 15th to date, which launched on Friday evening (Nov. 13). But Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel warning during its return to Starbase about 6.5 minutes after launch and autonomously diverted to splash down in the Gulf of Mexico. That wasn't a huge deal for SpaceX, as it had already caught Super Heavy on three previous test flights . Snagging Ship is tougher; the upper stage returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter than the booster does. SpaceX had not even attempted a Ship catch before Flight 15. But the company managed to pull off the maneuver on its first try. And Ship did some work in orbit before coming home: It deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites on Flight 15, the second batch that the company has sent to low Earth orbit . The first set was deployed on Flight 14 , which launched on Sept. 28.

item.title: Raye Tops the 2027 Grammy Nominations With 11 Including Album of the Year
item.description: Raye singing on stage with her band and backing vocalists. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram When the 2027 Grammy nominations dropped earlier this week, one name sat right at the top of the entire board: Raye . Out of every artist in the running for the 69th Annual Grammy Awards, she has the highest Grammy nominations this year with 11 nods, putting her ahead of Rosalía on nine. If you have been watching her rise over the past few years, seeing her command this much spotlight on music’s biggest stage feels well earned, especially for readers following global talent with Ghanaian roots through her mother’s side of the family. Her reaction online captured just how surreal the moment felt, writing on Instagram: “WHAT IS HAPPENING WHAT IS HAPPENING 11 GRAMMY NOMINATIONS INCLUDING ALBUM OF THE YEAR MY HEARTTTTT CANNOT EVEN FATHOM, MY HEARTTTTTTTT ” before following up with a simple “can’t stop crying .” Raye at home with her parents following the 2027 Grammy nominations announcement. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram In case you are still catching up on her story, Raye was born Rachel Keen in London to a Ghanaian-Swiss mother and an English father, and she has spent years building a reputation as a sharp songwriter, vocalist, and arranger who refuses to stay boxed into one sound. Many listeners first got to know her through chart-topping collaborations and pop hooks before she parted ways with her former major label to release music independently, taking full creative control of her catalogue and storytelling. That independent leap paid off massively—her album This Music May Contain Hope topped the UK chart in March 2026 and won the 2026 Mercury Prize in October, turning her into one of the most talked-about voices in music. Artwork for This Music May Contain Hope. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram Her 11 nominations for 2027 stretch right across her artistry, from songwriting and performance to arrangement, visuals, and full-length projects. This Music May Contain Hope is competing in both Album of the Year and Best Pop Vocal Album, while her hit “ WHERE IS MY HUSBAND! “—which reached UK No. 1 in January 2026—is up for Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Pop Solo Performance. She also earned nods for “ Click Clack Symphony ” alongside Hans Zimmer in Best Pop Duo/Group Performance, Best Arrangement, Instrumental and Vocals, and Best Music Video, plus “ Life Boat ” in Best Dance Pop Recording, “ I Hate the Way I Look Today” in Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance, and a Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical nod. Raye holding a number one award following a year of UK chart milestones, including “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!” hitting No. 1 in January 2026 and This Music May Contain Hope topping the UK chart in March 2026. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram This is not her first time on the Grammy radar, though it is easily her biggest moment yet. Before this sweep, Raye had four prior Grammy nominations—taking her career total to 15—including Best New Artist, Songwriter

item.title: No more asteroid landing: Engine trouble forces Japan's Hayabusa2 probe to change plans
item.description: null Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 mission, due to the spacecraft suffering trouble with its ion thrusters. The veteran Hayabusa2 spacecraft launched back in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu . Since delivering the samples to Earth in December 2020 via a reentry capsule, the main spacecraft has been conducting an extended mission of exploration and in July made a super-close flyby of the two-headed asteroid Torifune. But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end. The spacecraft was scheduled to rendezvous with, and attempt to land on, the tiny, 36-foot-wide (11 meters) near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031, but trouble with the aging spacecraft's engines has forced a change of plan. But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end. The spacecraft was scheduled to rendezvous with, and attempt to land on, the tiny, 36-foot-wide (11 meters) near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031, but trouble with the aging spacecraft's engines has forced a change of plan. The spacecraft will instead target 2015 BM510, another tiny asteroid. And there will be no landing: Hayabusa2 is scheduled to make a high-speed flyby of the near-Earth object in April 2028. The decision was announced at a Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) press conference on Tuesday (Nov. 17), a day after a Cabinet Office space policy subcommittee meeting. The final functioning thruster out of Hayabusa2's four ion engines suffered a malfunction in mid-August, according to JAXA officials, while a sensor detected unexpected erosion of the spacecraft's surface during its long voyage in space. "The deterioration of the onboard equipment ... is becoming increasingly evident," Japan Times quoted Yuya Mimasu, team leader of the extended mission, as saying. A size comparison between asteroid Ryugu, which was visited by Hayabusa2 in 2020, and its planned next target, 1998 KY26. The 2031 visit to 1998 KY26 is now off, however; Hayabusa2 will instead fly by a different small asteroid in 2028. (Image credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser. Asteroid models: T. Santana-Ros, JAXA/University of Aizu/Kobe University) Despite losing the opportunity to land on KY26, the Hayabusa2 mission has been a huge success for JAXA, and the new direction promises its own intrigues. Asteroid 2015 BM510 has already attracted interest; it's the primary target of a proposal for the European Space Agency 's mini-Fast mission series. Scientists describe the body as a D-type asteroid, meaning it's thought to be organic-rich and comet-like, and may have originated in the outer solar system. Around the same time as Hayabusa2 conducts its high-speed flyby in April 2028, JAXA is also scheduled to launch its next asteroid mission, Destiny+. item.title: A Safari, a Beach & Easy Entry? 5 African Spots for Your Christmas Holiday
item.description: Five African destinations Nigerian passport holders can visit visa-free or with visa on arrival this Christmas holiday. Image: AI-generated. The group chat has the concerts, the dinners and the Detty December link-ups covered. But has anyone planned the getaway? Beyond the usual Lagos parties and end-of-year outings, there is a whole continent waiting to be explored, with sun-soaked beaches, wildlife safaris, exciting food scenes and cities with plenty of stories to tell. You do not have to spend weeks navigating embassy appointments and visa applications to make it happen, either. Several African countries offer Nigerian passport holders visa-free entry or visas on arrival, making a festive-season escape much easier to plan. Whether you are travelling solo, gathering your friends, taking the family along or joining a curated travel group, here are five destinations worth considering for your Christmas holiday. Kenya Imagine spotting lions and giraffes against a city skyline before breakfast, then catching an evening flight or train straight to the coast for fresh seafood by the Indian Ocean. That contrast is what makes Kenya such a rewarding December escape. Nairobi gives you immediate access to wildlife at Nairobi National Park and the Giraffe Centre alongside lively restaurants and art spaces in Westlands and Karen, while longer itineraries open up classic game drives in the Maasai Mara, views of Mount Kilimanjaro in Amboseli, and warm beach days in Diani or Watamu. Nigerian citizens enjoy visa-free entry for short stays of up to 60 days without needing a paid eTA, leaving more room in your budget for safaris and coastal stays. Rwanda Not everyone wants their year-end holiday to feel like a non-stop sprint, and Rwanda is built for travellers who prefer scenery, clean air, and an unhurried pace. Days in Kigali easily revolve around specialty coffee shops, contemporary art at Inema Arts Center, and a sobering, essential visit to the Kigali Genocide Memorial before you head out into the countryside. From the capital, you can track chimpanzees and walk above the trees in Nyungwe Forest, go on wildlife drives in Akagera National Park, or spend quiet afternoons along the shores of Lake Kivu. With 30-day visa-free entry for Nigerian passport holders, getting there is straightforward from start to finish. Mauritius Sometimes a proper Christmas break calls for leaving mainland schedules behind altogether for turquoise lagoons, catamaran cruises, and mountain trails. In Mauritius, you can base yourself around Grand Baie in the north for boat trips to Île aux Cerfs and lively beachside dinners, or head south-west toward Le Morne Brabant for coastal hikes and water sports. Between beach days, the bustling Central Market in Port Louis, the lush trails of Black River Gorges National Park, and Casela Nature Parks keep a week-long itinerary full without ever feeling hectic. From the capital, you can track chimpanzees and walk above the trees in Nyungwe Forest, go on wildlife drives in Akagera National Park, or spend quiet afternoons along the shores of Lake Kivu. With 30-day visa-free entry for Nigerian passport holders, getting there is straightforward from start to finish. Mauritius Sometimes a proper Christmas break calls for leaving mainland schedules behind altogether for turquoise lagoons, catamaran cruises, and mountain trails. In Mauritius, you can base yourself around Grand Baie in the north for boat trips to Île aux Cerfs and lively beachside dinners, or head south-west toward Le Morne Brabant for coastal hikes and water sports. Between beach days, the bustling Central Market in Port Louis, the lush trails of Black River Gorges National Park, and Casela Nature Parks keep a week-long itinerary full without ever feeling hectic. Nigerian travellers receive a free 14-day visa on arrival, though you will need to fill out Mauritius’s free All-in-One Travel Digital Form and Health Declaration Form online before boarding. Ghana Staying close to home does not mean settling for the same routine, especially when Accra turns into one of West Africa’s busiest festive hubs every December. You can spend mornings browsing contemporary art at Gallery 1957 and walking through historic Jamestown, afternoons unwinding at Labadi Beach or Kokrobite, and nights hopping between concerts and street-food spots. Whenever you are ready for a change of scenery, a road trip to Cape Coast and Elmina brings historic castles and the treetop canopy walkway at Kakum National Park within easy reach, while Aburi and Akosombo offer cooler hills and riverside views. Thanks to ECOWAS free movement, Nigerian passport holders enter Ghana visa-free for up to 90 days by air or road. Côte d’Ivoire For a West African holiday with a distinct francophone rhythm, Côte d’Ivoire pairs cosmopolitan city life with laid-back coastal escapes just a short flight from Nigeria. Abidjan greets visitors with lagoon views, leafy walking trails inside Banco National Park, and vibrant late-night dining in Zone 4 and Cocody where grilled fish and attiéké steal the show. A quick drive east takes you to Grand-Bassam for quiet beaches, craft markets, and historic architecture, while Assinie offers resort-style downtime further along the coast. Covered under ECOWAS visa-free access for up to 90 days, it is an easy switch-up when you want familiar regional warmth with a fresh cultural flavour. item.title: China rolls out rocket for launch of 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station (video)
item.description: null China's space station is set to receive its first foreign astronaut. A Long March 2F rocket, topped with the Shenzhou-24 crew spacecraft, was rolled out to the pad at Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, on Tuesday (Nov. 17), with launch expected in the next week. The 191-foot-tall (58 meters) rocket was transferred 0.93 miles (1.5 kilometers) from a vertical integration building to the pad over the course of around two hours, starting around 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT, or 5 p.m. Beijing Time), according to China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026. (Image credit: CCTV) China's human spaceflight agency, CMSA, stated that all facilities and equipment at the launch site are in good condition, adding that the launch is scheduled to take place in the coming days, without providing a date. CMSA typically holds a press conference at Jiuquan a day ahead of launch, during which the crew for the mission is revealed to the public. This time, one of the three crew members will, for the first time, be an international astronaut. One of two Pakistani astronaut candidates will fly to the Tiangong space station on Shenzhou-24, marking a first both for China's outpost and for Pakistan, which will see one its astronauts reach orbit for the first time. Though public details are sparse, it is thought that the Pakistani astronaut, operating as a payload specialist, will stay aboard Tiangong for around a week, returning home on the departing Shenzhou-23 spacecraft. One of the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts — who are approaching the end of their six-month-long mission, having launched on May 24 — will stay aboard Tiangong for another half a year. This will provide the international visitor with a seat home on Shenzhou-23, and allow a Chinese astronaut to make the country's first year-long stay in orbit. This extra-long mission will supply China with data on physiology ahead of crewed lunar flights and other long-duration missions. China approved its human spaceflight program in 1992 and launched its first orbital crewed mission in 2003, with Yang Liwei becoming the first Chinese national in space. The country then completed the three-module Tiangong space station in late 2022 and has kept the orbital outpost constantly crewed ever since, with rotating six-month-long missions with brief handovers between crews. Shenzhou-24 will be China's 18th crewed mission and will mark the first time a foreign national is flying on a Shenzhou spacecraft. China is also looking to double the size of Tiangong in the coming years, potentially opening the way to further international missions and space tourist visits.

item.title: Don't miss Saturn shine close to the moon tonight
item.description: null The moon shines close to the ringed giant Saturn after sunset tonight (Nov. 20), presenting a spectacular naked-eye display as the stars of the Great Square of Pegasus twinkle nearby. Saturn's steady light will appear a little over 5 degrees from the 82%-lit moon in the southeastern sky after the sun dips below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length. Moonlight will hide fainter stars from view, though you should be able to spot Algenib, Markab, Alpheratz and Scheat arrayed in a diamond formation above the lunar disk, marking out the asterism of the Great Square of Pegasus in the November sky. The moon will present a spectacular target through the eyepiece of a 6-inch telescope, as the terminator line separating night from day creeps ever closer to its western edge. It's a great time to explore the 110 km-wide Gassendi Crater on the edge of Mare Humorum as its eastern rim and central peaks throw intense shadows across its interior. Gassendi Crater is a fascinating target for telescope observation during the moon's waxing gibbous phase. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva. Inset: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio.) Slewing your telescope over to Saturn will reveal details and subtle variations in the cloud surface of the gas giant , along with its iconic ring system, which is gradually becoming more visible following its ring plane crossing in March 2025. Depending on viewing conditions, you may also notice a shoal of bright, star-like points of light surrounding Saturn's disk, which represent the large moons Titan , Dione , Tethys , Rhea and Iapetus . Interested in seeing the planets of the solar system up close for yourself? Then be sure to check out our picks of the best telescopes available in 2026 , including the Celestron NexStar 8SE , which we rate as the best motorized scope out there. Editor's Note: If you would like to share your planetary astrophotography with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: Netflix's '3 Body Problem' season 2 trailer gives us a release date and a chilling warning: 'They are coming to exterminate us'
item.description: null " 3 Body Problem ," Netflix's unsettling adaptation of the first book in Chinese author Cixin Liu's epic alien invasion trilogy, "Remembrance of Earth’s Past," made a serious impact on viewers searching for hardcore E.T. drama and now an explosive new trailer for season 2 has just entered our orbit. This sensational saga about a malevolent interstellar society trying to exist within the unpredictable orbital mechanics of a planet and its triple sun system that forms an Earth-bound armada still has us a bit slack-jawed more than two years after debuting in 2024 . Now we're admittedly eager for this shortened 6-episode sophomore outing, which is officially arriving on Jan. 14, 2027. Delivered by Emmy Award-winning "Game of Thrones" team of David Benioff and D.B. Weiss and "True Blood's" Alexander Woo, "3 Body Problem" season 2 revolves around the combined forces of the Planetary Defense Council as they mount a daring deep space counterattack against the San-Ti. The San-Ti have arrived in Netflix's "3 Body Problem" season 2! (Image credit: Netflix) These Trisolarians are not the friendliest of galactic neighbors, and prior to the all-out invasion their primary goal was to thwart humanity’s ability to create advanced defense weaponry in the four centuries it would take for them to enter our solar system. This time it's more about the next phase of ultimate survival and dire actions taken by anti-alien and pro-alien factions. Season 2 leaps forward 400 years and focuses on the results of the Wallfacer Project, a secret initiative where chosen individuals worked on solutions in isolation as to not attract the attention of the Trisolarian's omnipresent AI surveillance technology called sophons. While the debut season was based on Liu's Hugo Award-winning 2008 novel, "The Three-Body Problem," this upcoming Netflix offering will adapt the second book, "The Dark Forest." 2010's "Death's End" closed out the acclaimed sci-fi trilogy. Netflix Netflix Netflix Netflix "So much of season 1 is about the mystery of what's happening," co-creator and co-executive producer David Benioff tells Netflix. "By the time season 2 starts, we have a lot more information. We know there is a hostile alien civilization out there, the San-Ti, and they’re coming our way, and they want our planet for themselves." Landing on Jan. 14, 2027, "3 Body Problem" season 2's international cast includes returners Jess Hong, Benedict Wong, Jovan Adepo, Eiza González, Liam Cunningham, Marlo Kelly, Sea Shimooka, Saamer Usmani, Alex Sharp and Josh Brener. Joining them are fresh cast members Claudia Doumit, Ellie de Lange, Alfie Allen, David Yip and Jordan Sunshine. Watch 3 Body Problem on Netflix: Standard with ads: $8.99/month Standard: $19.99/month Premium (4K): $26.99/month

item.title: Football Daily | Football’s political gamers face off at Fifa with the real-life final boss
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Although the millions of gamers who are pulling sickies would beg to differ, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI wasn’t the most exciting midnight launch involving a sprawling enterprise full of shady characters. Over in Zurich, the clock also struck 12 on the candidate deadline for next year’s Fifa presidential election, leaving those of us who have no interest in video games with our own chaotic, multi-billion-dollar sandbox where untouchable bosses bend the rules to suit themselves. While online carjackers are busy exploring a “most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world” , football’s real-life power brokers are gearing up for a March showdown in the actual city of Rabat. When I first saw the photo in yesterday’s Football Daily , I thought Mauricio Pochettino had opted for a short back and sides, presumably to pre-empt him tearing his luscious locks out in frustration at forthcoming poor results/terrible January transfer window/petulant sniping from sulky squad members. Then I realised he was in the back seat, all but entirely obscured by the rear-view mirror, in which he could perhaps see his sense of job satisfaction disappearing …” – Phil Taverner. That photo of Pochettino being chauffeured by a beefy driver answered one of my burning questions: what’s Ange Postecoglou doing these days?” – Mike Wilner (and others). This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...
